blocks.text: Stage Two: Taking Precepts as the Foundation

inline.s: The texts studied in this stage are the Sutra of the Forty-Two Chapters, the Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings, the Sutra of the Ten Wholesome Karmic Paths, the Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching, and the Great Mindfulness Sutra. The core of this stage's study is: "Take refuge in the Three Jewels, observe all the precepts in full, and never violate the rules of dignity."

The companion commentaries are: Annotated Sutra of the Forty-Two Chapters, Annotated Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings, Annotated Sutra of the Ten Wholesome Karmic Paths, Annotated Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching, and Annotated Great Mindfulness Sutra.

Practice: First, hear, reflect, and cultivate. Second, take turns reciting the Sutra of the Forty-Two Chapters, the Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings, the Sutra of the Ten Wholesome Karmic Paths, the Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching, and the Great Mindfulness Sutra, one each day. Third, be aware of the breath and aware of the sensations (see the book Awareness Chan for details).

rows.s: Annotated Sutra of the Forty-Two Chapters

This sutra is the first Buddhist scripture to be transmitted to our land. Its content is at once shallow and deep, gradual and sudden, partial and perfect, provisional and real, and includes both the Lesser and the Greater Vehicles. It is a scripture of outline and principle. This commentary helps the reader grasp the meaning within the text.
Annotated Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings

The Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings sets out to clarify the eight realizations of the bodhisattva (the "great beings" of the sutra): the realization of impermanence and no-self, the realization of few desires and non-doing, the realization of contented poverty and guarding the Way, the realization of constant diligence, the realization of wide learning and growth in wisdom, the realization of even-mindedness toward enemies and kin, the realization of the harm of the five desires, and the realization of the great mind of universal deliverance, so as to awaken oneself and awaken others. This commentary helps the reader grasp the meaning within the text.
Annotated Sutra of the Ten Wholesome Karmic Paths

In the Sutra of the Ten Wholesome Karmic Paths the Buddha says that all dharmas are never apart from the mind, and that one should cultivate the ten wholesome acts and sever all suffering. This is the most fundamental practice of the Buddha's teaching. This commentary helps the reader grasp the meaning within the text.
Annotated Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching

The Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching is the final instruction the Buddha gave to his disciples before entering nirvana. There he singles out the essence and reiterates, in earnest, how to cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom so as to escape affliction and birth-and-death. This commentary helps the reader grasp the meaning within the text.
Annotated Great Mindfulness Sutra

In the study of Buddhism what matters most is actual practice and real realization, putting an end to birth-and-death and escaping the round of rebirth. Hence the first task is to subdue affliction and then to sever it. For a student of the Pure Land school, as long as one can subdue affliction, one can single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name and be reborn in the Western Pure Land. In the Great Mindfulness Sutra the Buddha gives a full and detailed teaching on how to subdue affliction and sever it: to maintain an unbroken, continuous awareness and contemplation of the arising and ceasing and changing of body, mind, and world. This is the simplest and most direct method of going from the knowledge of suffering to the ending of suffering. This commentary helps the reader grasp the meaning within the text.

inline.s: The texts studied in this stage are the Diamond Sutra, the Heart Sutra, the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, and the Direct Explanation of the True Mind. The core of this stage's study is: "Rouse the bodhi mind, deeply believe in cause and effect, recite the Mahayana scriptures, and encourage fellow cultivators."

The companion commentaries are: Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra, Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra, Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, and Detailed Explanation of the Direct Explanation of the True Mind.

Practice: First, hear, reflect, and cultivate. Second, recite the Diamond Sutra and the Heart Sutra once each every day. Third, be aware of the mind's thoughts (see the book Awareness Chan for details).

rows.s: Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra

For a thousand years, why has the Diamond Sutra been known in every household, expounded in countless lectures, and annotated countless times? The reason lies not only in the immeasurable merit and virtue gained by receiving, upholding, and reciting it, but also because people have come to realize that the Diamond Sutra reveals a truth of boundless yet most mysterious power, a wish-fulfilling king of jewels for leaving suffering, escaping death, and attaining Buddhahood. Therefore they pursue and contemplate it tirelessly: What is the Diamond Sutra speaking of? What, indeed, is it speaking of? To answer these questions, this explanation was composed.

The commentary in this book is thorough and lucid. On the one hand it helps the reader grasp the meaning of the original text, and on the other it helps students improve their ability to read classical prose, laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra

The Heart Sutra is on everyone's lips, for it is the great dharma that destroys illusion and carries all beings beyond all suffering and calamity. When Master Xuanzang journeyed west in search of the scriptures, he crossed alone an eight-hundred-li desert of yellow sand, where no bird flew above and no beast walked below, and he often encountered all manner of ghosts and demons of monstrous shapes thronging before and behind him; yet the master "thought only of the Heart Sutra, and at the sound of it they vanished at once." This shows that the Heart Sutra is not only exquisite in meaning, but also that receiving, upholding, and reciting it takes effect most marvelously. However, the meaning of this sutra is profound and hard to grasp; if the meaning is not reached, the contemplative view is unclear; and if the contemplative view is unclear, one wanders in confusion with no direction. For this reason this explanation was composed.

The commentary in this book is thorough and lucid. On the one hand it helps the reader grasp the meaning of the original text, and on the other it helps students improve their ability to read classical prose, laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch is the only work of Chinese Buddhism honored with the title "sutra." It sets forth systematically and comprehensively the theory and practice of the sudden teaching of "seeing one's nature and realizing Buddhahood," and its appearance marks the formal establishment of the Chan school in China, blazing with a ten-thousand-rayed light. The Platform Sutra is the great practice of the Diamond Sutra and the Heart Sutra. The Diamond Sutra and the Heart Sutra speak of the true reality of all dharmas, while the Platform Sutra, drawing on them, uses concrete practice to realize that true reality, accomplish the patience with the unborn, and so reach the perfect clarity that forever leaves all marks and directly attains Buddhahood.

This book provides a detailed commentary. On the one hand it helps the reader grasp the meaning of the original text, and on the other it helps students improve their ability to read classical prose, laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Selected Annotations on the Buddha-Store Sutra

In the study of the Buddha-dharma, the first requirement is proper view. What is proper view? To take the scriptures as one's basis, the Buddha's mind as one's own mind, the Buddha's words as one's own words, and the Buddha's conduct as one's own conduct. That is proper view. To this end, the "Chapter on the True Reality of All Dharmas, First," the "Chapter on Buddha-Recollection, Second," the "Chapter on Pure Dharma, Sixth," the "Chapter on the Ancient Past, Seventh," and the "Chapter on the Ascertainment of Precepts, Ninth" have been chosen from the Buddha-Store Sutra and annotated.
Detailed Explanation of the Direct Explanation of the True Mind

The Direct Explanation of the True Mind treats the true mind (the inherent nature) comprehensively under the following fifteen aspects: the right faith of the true mind, the other names of the true mind, the wondrous substance of the true mind, the wondrous functioning of the true mind, the unity and difference of substance and function, the true mind in delusion, the true mind stilling delusion, the four postures of the true mind, where the true mind dwells, the true mind's escape from death, the primary and auxiliary practices, the virtue of the true mind, the verification of the true mind's merit, the true mind's non-knowing, and where the true mind goes. It clarifies the true mind (the inherent nature) that everyone inherently possesses, the root of delusion and awakening, and the path of practice and the state attained.

blocks.text: Stage Four: Concentration and Wisdom in Equal Practice

inline.s: The texts studied in this stage are: Detailed Explanation of the Treatise on the Two Entries and Four Practices, Detailed Explanation of the Essentials of Mind Cultivation, Essentials of Chan and Pure Land, and The Essential Mind of White Cloud (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation).
Practice: First, read and apply hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Second, meditate (see the book Awareness Chan for details).
[Equal practice of concentration and wisdom] The Treatise on Severing Contemplation says:
"When the mind-nature is still and extinct, this is concentration; always realizing this still extinction is wisdom."

This means: when the mind-nature dwells in a state of still extinction, it is called concentration; knowing clearly at all times that the mind-nature is in this still extinction is called wisdom. Therefore concentration is stillness, and wisdom is illumination. To hold concentration and wisdom in equal practice is to be still yet illuminating, illuminating yet still. Master Dayu says:
"In stillness and illumination, in illumination and stillness, beware above all of forcing; to become a Buddha or a patriarch there is no other secret."
In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment the Buddha says:
"All Tathagatas, in their originating ground, rely upon the perfect illumination of the pure, clear awareness-image and forever sever ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha-way."

Here, the pure, clear awareness-image is concentration, and perfect illumination is wisdom; the perfect illumination of the pure, clear awareness-image is precisely the equal practice of concentration and wisdom.

[Stillness-illumination] Still yet illuminating: when a single thought does not arise (stillness), to be aware that this single thought does not arise (illumination) is like a pearl emitting light that still shines back upon the pearl's own body. Stillness is the substance, illumination the substance's functioning. Concentration is the substance, wisdom the substance's functioning. [Originating ground] This refers to the time when the Buddha was on the causal ground. [Causal ground] From the stage of an ordinary being first rousing the mind to study Buddhism up to the perfect realization of Buddhahood, the whole process is called the "causal ground."

rows.s: Detailed Explanation of the Treatise on the Two Entries and Four Practices

The Treatise on the Two Entries and Four Practices is the essential teaching on entering the Way that Patriarch Bodhidharma transmitted personally. The words are few but the meaning is rich, embracing both principle and practice; truly it is the outline of the school and the guide of the practitioner. This book provides a detailed commentary. On the one hand it helps the reader grasp the meaning of the original text, and on the other it helps students improve their ability to read classical prose, laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Detailed Explanation of the Essentials of Mind Cultivation

The Essentials of Mind Cultivation explains the essential method of mind cultivation from three aspects: seeing one's nature and realizing Buddhahood, sudden awakening with gradual cultivation, and the equal practice of concentration and wisdom. First, the aim of seeing one's nature lies in realizing that one's own mind is the true Buddha and one's own nature is the true Dharma. Second, to see through that the ordinary being is the Buddha is sudden awakening; to be transformed by the power of the Dharma is gradual cultivation. The tracks of the thousand sages are no more than these two gates. Third, empty stillness and numinous knowing are the substance (concentration) and functioning (wisdom) of the inherent nature; therefore one should be ever still and ever knowing, with substance and functioning never apart, holding concentration and wisdom in equal practice.

This book provides a detailed commentary. On the one hand it helps the reader grasp the meaning of the original text, and on the other it helps students improve their ability to read classical prose, laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
The Essential Mind of White Cloud (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation)

The distinguishing feature of The Essential Mind of White Cloud (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation) is that it is keen, swift, sudden, and perfect. How great the good fortune of those who read it and practice it! One should advance with understanding and practice together, understanding in the very act of practice, and practice in the very act of understanding. Do the work of taming the mind day by day: when the thoughts become clear, wisdom is born; never apart from the inherent nature is the field of merit. When one contemplates until a single thought does not arise, one is in accord with prajna. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "All Tathagatas, in their originating ground, rely upon the perfect illumination of the pure, clear awareness-image and forever sever ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha-way."

This book provides a detailed commentary. On the one hand it helps the reader grasp the meaning of the original text, and on the other it helps students improve their ability to read classical prose, laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Essentials of Chan and Pure Land

Master Hanshan says: "In the age of the Dharma's end there are many who practice, yet few who gain the real benefit; many who toil with great effort, yet few who gain real power. Why is this? It is because they do not light upon a direct point at which to begin."

The Essentials of Chan and Pure Land is compiled from Master Hanshan's Collection of Dream-Wandering, and it focuses on how to practice in earnest. In its several chapters Master Hanshan gives incisive teachings on the essentials and the points of entry of both the Chan and the Pure Land schools. As students savor them repeatedly and advance in understanding and practice together, they will surely gain the real benefit.

This book provides a detailed commentary. On the one hand it helps the reader grasp the meaning of the original text, and on the other it helps students improve their ability to read classical prose, laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment has twelve chapters, in which the Buddha, through dialogue with twelve great bodhisattvas, proclaims the wondrous principle of the Tathagata's perfect enlightenment (the perfect awakening of the inherent nature) and the method of practice.

Master Hanshan says: "As for what is most simple yet most refined, most immediate yet most essential, nothing surpasses the supreme Dharma-gate of perfect enlightenment. Its text is no more than thirteen thousand words, yet it unites the boundless ocean of teachings and encompasses the whole Dharma-realm; it rounds to the single source of the mind and passes through the purport of the three contemplations. Partial and proper interchanged, single and repeated cultivated in fullness, it exhausts the lord of delusion, strips away the maladies of Chan, and the wondrous gate of awakening the mind surmounts directly in a single leap. This is what is called the true sutra of the Dharma-realm, the wondrous practice of becoming a Buddha. Sudden awakening and sudden realization are like viewing a fruit in one's palm. The purport of the coming from the West, the secret and wondrous meaning, holds nothing beyond this. All who study Buddhism take it as their guide." (From the Postscript to the Engraved Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment)
Awareness Chan

This is the practice textbook of the Chan School, whose aim is: ten thousand thoughts converge into one, and the one returns to nothingness, thereby seeing one's nature and realizing Buddhahood. As for how to investigate Chan, this book gives a systematic explanation and concrete steps of practice, truly as the ancients said: "In its cultivation there is a step by which to enter; in its realization there is a truth one obtains for oneself."
